1:
The date looks self-contradictory and is not. Henry explains that the first four years could be called the beginning of the reign, the king holding his throne as a tributary through them; the rebellion came after. In this same year he travelled to Babylon in person, which raised hopes that his errand would end the war — hopes the false prophets fed. Wesley suspects a reckoning by the sabbatical cycle. Clarke fixes the fifth month to the new moon of August and notes that the verse dates the preceding chapter too, settling that the royal name at its head is wrong — a copyist's slip, Ellicott agrees.

Gibeon repays attention, and Ellicott takes three things from it. It lay in the prophet's own tribe a few miles out, so the quarrel in the capital may be an old rivalry revived. It was a priests' town, so Hananiah was probably a priest too — Clarke and Wesley agree. And it had once held the tabernacle, brought there after the ark was lost from Shiloh, and seen a king's accession sacrifice; a man raised among those relics, Ellicott suggests, should have learned that no place is exempt. He guesses the day was a feast, the courts crowded.

The crowd heard the true prophet's own formula in another mouth. Ellicott hears deliberate irony: the word for breaking picks up the symbol just made famous, and the same divine titles are claimed. Gill notes he described the Lord exactly as the genuine messengers do, a bold and daring act; Clarke calls it awful impudence in a man who knew he had no commission. Henry adds the staging: the challenger faced Jeremiah and addressed the speech to him, which amounted to calling him a public liar.

Calvin dwells on where the man stood. The sanctuary was around him, the ark before him, everywhere said to carry the divine presence; the title he invoked names not only eternal being but power spread through heaven and earth. To announce a lie there should have felled him had he been harder than iron. Calvin then asks what the narrative leaves open — knowing fraud or sincere bigot, ambition or delusion — and answers that either way he served one master, whose kind is not extinct. The divine name was tossed between two claimants as though the devil played with it; but the godly could tell them apart, since one delivered orders and the other courted applause.

The term set is examined closely. Ellicott renders it literally two years of days, notes that the challenger grew bolder as he grew precise, and observes that with no sign offered the hearers could judge only by the lives of the two men, which is the test the law lays down. Calvin insists it means within the two years, not at their end, a range naming no particular day, and sets the two against the seventy already assigned. Clarke finds a grim irony: the interval gave the enemy time to finish the city, and the man who named it did not see it out.

Naming the exiled king reveals the politics. Ellicott reads a programme in it — the reigning king deposed as too compliant, the young captive restored as figurehead of resistance, all resting on Egyptian support. Gill sees why it would please a people who thought their present king a deputy rather than a sovereign, and why he would have to feign approval. Calvin presses the awkwardness: restoration required an abdication, and the speaker gambled on popular feeling and on a ruler who knew his title weak, not holding the throne by succession. Henry weighs the speech and finds the piety missing — prosperity promised without a word of repentance or prayer, temporal mercies detached from the spiritual ones that always accompany them, the spirit of the world in a man aiming to please, not profit.
5:
Calvin sets up the reply by explaining why it was needed. A people handled roughly does not listen; men want flattery, cannot bear being called to account, grow indignant when their faults are named, and shy from any unwelcome rumour. The prophet's commission was twofold, to expose the vices that made them unworthy of the land and to announce the sentence, and he had to do both without being written off as an enemy of his own nation.

Hence the Amen, and the expositors divide over its tone. Gill takes it plainly: as a countryman he wished the thing true, as a prophet he knew it could not be, and what he really wanted was the repentance that would make the threat needless and the promise possible. Clarke reads it as an open-hearted wish that the people might find it so. Ellicott denies both, hearing keen and incisive irony — the wish could be echoed honestly as a wish, but the speaker knew it impossible, since the whole state of things would have to change first, and thinks it unwise to pray for what runs against the declared purpose of God.

Calvin explains how the two attitudes coexist without hypocrisy. The prophets were given a heroic greatness of mind that let them set their countrymen aside and deliver whatever was commanded, however grievous; but they did not put off ordinary human feeling with it. So the same man could wish his people well and go on announcing a decree that neither he nor any mortal could alter. Calvin insists on both halves, because a messenger without the first turns coward and one without the second turns barbarous.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the argument as a piece of reasoning: the fulfilment is granted to be desirable, and then the record is put in evidence — every prophet of the Lord down to that day had spoken of war and calamity, so that a man who predicts nothing but safety stands against the whole line of witnesses. Ellicott calls this frankly inductive. The older prophets whose names were honoured had not spoken smooth things, which gives an antecedent probability to the one speaking in the same tone now, and throws the burden of proof on those holding out flattering hopes. Gill and Clarke both fill in the roll of those earlier voices, and agree that all of them denounced the same evils on a corrupt people.

Calvin pauses over the wording. The middle term of the three evils ought to be famine, he thinks, and he notes that more than twenty manuscripts read it so, though the versions run the other way; he would also repeat the verb, so that the sentence says the prophets who spoke against many lands and mighty kingdoms spoke of war and famine and pestilence, with no claim about prophets who did not address the nations at all.

The criterion itself is stated most sharply by Clarke. A true prophet names the thing and fixes the term, and both come out as named; and he sets the two claims side by side, two years for the return of vessels and captives against one year for the city's fall and seventy before any restoration. Ellicott notes that the word for peace covers every kind of national wellbeing, so it stands opposed to famine and plague as much as to war, and hears behind the whole test the language of the law, whose impress he finds all over this prophet. Calvin accepts the rule but refuses to let it stand alone: elsewhere the same law warns that a prediction may come true and the man still not be believed, the event being a trial of faith rather than a certificate, since impostors sometimes tell the truth. Gill adds only that a preacher of prosperity is always agreeable to his hearers.
10:
Seizing the yoke is the real offence. Gill calls it impudent and insolent, the worse because the thing was made and worn at command. Henry sees a calculated affront: breaking it produced a sign to answer the sign already given, and appeared to beat his opponent on his own ground. Calvin calls the act sacrilege, since the cords were the visible attestation God added for a people too dull to be moved by words; the prophet accepted the disgrace of wearing them so that they might work, and the band was in effect a sacrament securing credit for the message.

What the gesture reveals about its author interests Calvin most: once a man dares resist the word of God, and would unseat him if he could, he spares none of the emblems of that power. Henry finds the imitation as telling: the lying spirit borrows the very formula of the Spirit of truth, and lies are fathered on the God of truth as though that were nothing new. Whether the man believed his own message or knew it false and worked only on his hearers, Henry says the text does not tell us; what is plain is the assurance. Clarke puts it in one line: the acted sign was meant to make the prediction credible.

Calvin presses the craft of it. The impostor did not merely assert; he set a sign before the people and attached teaching to it, the true prophets' own method. That is what makes him dangerous: he could deceive people who were not stupid — Calvin contrasts the empty ceremonies he saw in the church of Rome, which please the eye and neglect the ear, whereas this man supplied both, added the divine name, and spoke as though God were the speaker. The answer is not that such mimicry is impossible but that discernment is given to those who ask humbly.

His restraint gets attention too. He simply walked away; Henry notes that being reviled he did not revile again, and would not wrangle with a man at the height of his fury before a hostile crowd. Calvin makes the silence policy: prolonging the quarrel would have kindled contention on every side, and nothing can be heard in a tumult, so the pearls were withheld and the holy name spared further insolence. Returning later under a fresh commission, he came back with authority a shouting match would have cost him. Calvin observes that Jeremiah keeps granting his opponent the title of prophet, knowing how scandalous it is that a man so acknowledged should serve the other side.

Ellicott reads the interval as silent suffering and prayer answered. Gill supposes he had retired to his lodging, and leaves open whether the word came by vision, dream, audible voice or an impulse on the spirit. Keil and Delitzsch place the commission not long after the departure and treat what follows as the Lord's formal testimony against the man.

The reply keeps the same image and turns it. Ellicott states the principle: resistance to a power that was for the time the scourge and so the servant of God could only produce a heavier bondage, and he hears in the iron yoke an echo of the law's curse. Clarke says as much practically: subjection tightened rather than lifted, property taken, even the livestock. Wesley reduces it to a sentence: the gesture incensed God further and made the judgment heavier. Calvin worries at the grammar, the first clause reporting what was to be said and the second what the prophet was told to do; he would read it as the Greek version does, the making of the iron yokes in the first person, a difference of one letter, and remarks that the requirement of a passage is among our best guides. Gill notes what had been abused: the name, the messenger, the message, its emblems.
14:
Calvin will not let the iron band stand as bare theatre. Worn without a word it would have been vain spectacle; explained, it persuaded many and left the hardened without excuse. He asks why the material changed, and answers that the crowd had endorsed the profanation of the wooden sign by their own consent, so it came back heavier. From this he draws a working rule: those who bark at God gain nothing but a doubled sentence, like a snared dog that struggles until it strangles itself. Gill notes that the titles used are the standing ones for a message committed to a prophet, and Ellicott passes over the clause about the livestock, explained a chapter earlier.

Where the two men met is not said. Gill guesses a public place, the point being as much the conviction of onlookers as the confusion of the man; Ellicott infers an interval of some days since the temple scene, and finds a strange significance in the same official title being given to true and false alike. Clarke measures the courage it took, with priests and people already partial to the man who told them what they liked — in such cases, he says, men wish to be deceived.

Calvin generalises the necessity of the confrontation. Plain teaching lacks weight while a loud opponent is left standing, and he applies it to his own day: when unprincipled men vomit out what darkens religion we must contend, or our teaching does nothing, since simple minds fluctuate while they see two parties in conflict. He then admires the brevity of the answer. A long speech was available, and the Spirit could have supplied it, but one charge ends all boasting whatever mask is worn: the man had not been sent.

The sentence is read with care. Ellicott points out that the verb is literally I send thee, the same word as in the accusation and repeated with pointed irony, and that the term allowed leaves room for repentance; he suspects too that shame at exposure may have helped bring on what was threatened. He classes it with the commission to root out and pull down, and sets beside it the strokes that fell on Ananias and on Elymas. Clarke turns it into a public test — not seventy years, not two years, but this year and within two months — while Calvin sees a mercy to the perplexed, who could not otherwise have judged between the claimants, and a stopping of mouths that had pleaded ignorance. On the closing charge Calvin gathers the versions, revolt or iniquity or perverseness or prevarication, and reports the explanation that by lying tales the man had encouraged people to hold out against warnings already given.

The death settles it, and the commentators measure what it settled. Gill states the bare logic: he died in the year named, which proved one man false and the other true. Clarke dates it to the seventh month against the fifth for the prophecy and calls the interval mercy, two months to prepare to meet a judge, adding that the fulfilment must have won credit for everything else the true prophet had said. Wesley draws the lesson for ministers who teach against a revealed will. Calvin is struck by the manner of it: no hand was laid on the man, no execution ordered, and he was driven out of the world by the sound of a tongue, as though the blow had come from heaven. What astonishes Calvin is that it changed nothing. He reports, and dismisses, the rabbinic suggestion that the body was secretly removed so the people never learned of the death; the narrative treats the event as public knowledge, and the blindness that followed it was chosen.
